Direct-acting electric radiators (also called electric resistance heaters) convert virtually 100 % of the electricity they draw into heat at the point of use. In that narrow sense, they are “efficient” at releasing heat into the room. However, when assessing overall energy efficiency and operating cost, two important points must be considered:

1. Primary energy and carbon footprint  
   • Electricity generation and distribution always incur losses (the “primary energy factor”). In many regions, generating each kilowatt-hour of electricity requires significantly more energy input from fuels (coal, gas, nuclear or renewables) than you get at the socket.  
   • If your electricity mix includes fossil fuels, the effective CO₂ emissions per kWh delivered can be higher than for district heating or modern heat pumps.

   • Over time, savings on your utility bills can offset the initial investment in the system.

   • Solar power is generated without burning fossil fuels, so it produces no direct carbon dioxide or air-polluting emissions.  
   • By using solar electricity you help reduce overall greenhouse-gas emissions.

   • Generating your own electricity protects you against rising energy prices and utility rate fluctuations.  
   • In combination with a battery-storage system, solar panels can provide backup power during grid outages.

Control- and regulation technology in a building-services context refers to the hardware and software systems that continuously measure, decide and act on the operation of HVAC, lighting, ventilation and other installations in order to

• Maintain occupants’ comfort (temperature, humidity, air quality, illumination)  
• Protect equipment and the building fabric  
• Optimize energy use and reduce operating costs  

Key components are:  
1. Sensors – record temperatures, CO₂ levels, flow rates, light levels, etc.  
2. Controllers – process sensor signals and execute control logic (e.g. on/off, PID loops)  
3. Actuators – carry out adjustments by modulating valves, dampers, fans, pumps or stretches of dimmable lighting  

Together they form closed-loop control circuits: a sensor detects a change, the controller computes the corrective action, and the actuator implements it. This automation ensures buildings stay comfortable, safe and energy-efficient without constant manual intervention.

• Normal (AC) charging  
  – Slow AC: up to about 3.7 kW (single-phase, typical home outlet)  
  – Fast AC (sometimes called “semi-fast”): roughly 3.7 – 22 kW (three-phase)  
  – In most discussions, any AC charging up to 22 kW is grouped as “standard” or “normal.”  

• Fast (DC) charging  
  – Begins at around 50 kW and today extends up to 350 kW or more with ultra-fast chargers.  
  – Uses an external DC charger (e.g. CCS, CHAdeMO) that bypasses the onboard charger.  

Boundary summary  
– Anything ≤ 22 kW (AC) is treated as normal charging.  
– Anything ≥ 50 kW (DC) is treated as fast charging.

As general background knowledge, “load balancing” in the context of electric-vehicle (EV) charging refers to the process of distributing the available electrical capacity intelligently among multiple charging points so that

• The total power drawn never exceeds the capability of the local grid connection or the building’s electrical installation  
• Each vehicle receives as much charging power as possible without overloading the system  
• Peak demand charges and the risk of circuit breakers tripping are minimized

In practice this involves measuring airflow rates at each terminal, adjusting dampers and fan speeds, and sometimes re‐sizing ducts or diffusers. When done correctly, balancing ensures that:

•  Supply and extract volumes are equal.  An unbalanced system either over-ventilates (wasting energy heating or cooling more air than needed) or under-ventilates (risking poor indoor air quality).  
•  Heat‐recovery devices (in heat-recovery ventilation systems) operate at their rated efficiency, transferring the maximum amount of thermal energy from exhaust air to incoming fresh air.
